records.title: City Attorney Opinion on CCFN 260142 (6.29.26)
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: Regulation and Potential Ban of Data Centers Dear Alderwoman Dimitrijevic:

This responds to your June 22, 2026 request for an opinion from the City Attorney’s Office regarding why the proposed substitute ordinance relating to the building of data centers (Common Council File No. 260142, proposed substitute A attached) is more advisable from a legal risk perspective than a ban on all data centers of any size in the city.
Data Centers Two particular attributes of data centers are essential to this analysis.
First, the term “data center” does not account for scale — a closet with half a dozen servers or a warehouse with ten thousand are both equally “data centers” at their core.

There are small data centers in a way that there are not small correctional facilities or material reclamation facilities, which are examples of uses in the city’s zoning code that are not permitted in any district.

Second, some would argue that data centers above a certain scale draw large quantities of power, generate significant amounts of noise, and require cooling systems that can waste vast amounts of water.

Because a “data center” includes uses so minor they could be freely done anywhere and so intense they might not be allowable anywhere in the city, regulation of data centers must reasonably account for both extremes, and its classifications must be supported by a record of reliable evidence.

Second, and more importantly, the proposed ordinance is more likely to withstand a legal challenge because it is tailored to address specific public welfare concerns that arise from the various types and sizes of data centers being regulated.

A court is more likely to find that the regulations in the proposed ordinance are designed to actually accomplish a purpose within the scope of the city’s police power, as opposed to a wholesale ban which fails to distinguish between data centers that pose little risk to the health, safety, or welfare of the public, and those that pose greater risk (whether because of their size, noise, or energy use).

Although only a few municipalities across the country have enacted complete bans on data centers, a lawsuit filed March 31, 2026 in Tennessee federal court by ExoticRidge Crypto Company against Hawkins County provides some insight into potential legal claims in response to a complete ban.
ExoticRidge alleges that Hawkins County violated the constitution by banning all data centers and cryptocurrency mining em masse, without regard to the actual impact of any particular project.

The text of the Hawkins County ban claims the massive amounts of electricity required to power cryptocurrency mining and large-scale data centers and the continuous industrial noise from the generators, cooling systems, and ventilation equipment are incompatible with the county’s rural character and the peaceful enjoyment of property by the county’s residents and that such operations typically create little to no sustainable economic benefit to the local community, employing minimal staff while imposing significant environmental and infrastructure burdens.

records.title: American Lung Association Support 7.28.26
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: Communities across Wisconsin are seeing data centers proposed at a record pace.
Unfortunately, when data centers are powered by dirty energy, they can put lung health at risk.
More demand for data centers – for AI, cryptocurrency, data hosting and other needs – means more demand for electricity.
We Energies has not retired the coal plants that had been slated to come offline in 2024.
Plus, many data centers use diesel generators for backup power on-site, subjecting local residents to cancer-causing particle pollution.
With over 4,000 data centers across the United States – and thousands more planned – energy demand is only growing.

It is critical that data center power needs not add local pollution burdens and instead developers should ensure that new, non-combustion renewable energy resources are available for both baseline and backup power.
Data centers must be developed with sensitivity to local utility consumer costs, regional air quality and broader sustainability needs.

Data centers do play a role in our economy and our lives, but we should SLOW DOWN and develop a common-sense plan to protect ourselves and our earth.

records.title: CPC Staff Report
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: This substitute ordinance would create a temporary pause in the establishment of new data centers or enlargement of existing data centers for one year, or until the Zoning Code is amended to formally define and regulate data centers.

This ordinance finds that the unprecedented recent national growth in the construction of data centers poses new and unique implications to communities, including impacts to energy and water infrastructure, the environment, and the public health, safety, and welfare.

Cities and states across the country are struggling to determine how to regulate this new and unique land use, and the Common Council intends for data centers to exist in harmony with the City’s existing Citywide Policy Plan, including the Climate & Equity Plan.

A separate Common Council File that would create a more long-term regulatory structure for data centers within the Zoning Code has been introduced and begun the process of public review and discussion (File No. 260142).
That separate ordinance would amend the City’s Zoning Code to establish a regulatory framework for data centers.

However, until that framework can be established, the sponsors of this pending pause ordinance seek to temporarily prohibit the building of new data centers until such time as the City’s Zoning Code is amended to accommodate this new type of land use.
At the present time, the City of Milwaukee’s Zoning Code does not specifically regulate data center land uses.

The proposed pause legislation is intended to serve as stopgap measure, allowing for the City to best protect public health, safety, and welfare, while working to establish a regulatory framework for data centers and to ensure future data center developments’ harmony with the City of Milwaukee’s Citywide Policy Plan and Climate & Equity Plan.

In this ordinance, “data center” means a facility, other than a transmission tower, used primarily to operate, maintain, or provide access to computer and network facilities for the transmission of voice, data, text, internet, sound, or full- motion-picture video between network termination points, together with accessory uses and facilities such as offices, air handlers, power generators, generator fuel storage, water cooling and storage facilities, and utility infrastructure that supports sustained operation of the data center.

Data center 251924 – 809 North Broadway, Milwaukee, WI 53202-3617 ZCTC Data Center Moratorium ● Phone (414) 286-5800 ● www.milwaukee.gov/dcd 09/28/26 CPC Milwaukee Business Information: www.choosemilwaukee.com shall not mean a computer server room or data facility that serves another principal use on the same premises.

No city department, board, commission, agency, or officer shall accept for filing, review, processing, or approval any application, permit request, occupancy request, zoning request, site-plan submission, or similar request seeking to establish, construct, enlarge, expand, convert, or occupy a data center during the effective period of this ordinance.

This prohibition shall apply regardless of how the facility is defined in the application materials, provided that the proposed principal use meets the definition of a data center, as defined in Part 1.

records.title: MMAC Oppose
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: We appreciate the Council’s interest in establishing a clear framework for evaluating data center development, and we share the goal of ensuring that any project in Milwaukee is a good neighbor.

The ordinance establishes a one-year prohibition on accepting applications related to the establishment or development of data centers or continues prohibition until the City's zoning code is amended to specifically regulate data centers.

MMAC strongly opposes this proposal because a pause of up to one year would effectively shut Milwaukee out of new data center investment while other communities continue to compete for these projects.
Data centers are the physical backbone of the modern economy.

Billions of dollars in data center investment are now under construction or planned in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington, Beaver Dam, and other communities, generating thousands of construction jobs and transformative growth in local tax bases.

Earlier this year, the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin approved a rate structure requiring the largest data center customers to pay the full cost of the new generation and fuel needed to serve them, expressly protecting existing residential and business ratepayers.

Milwaukee needs sustained growth in its property tax base to fund the services residents depend on, and data centers are among the highest-value, lowest-service-demand land uses available, significant taxable investment that adds little burden on schools, streets, or public safety.

records.title: City Attorney Opinion on CCFN 260142 (6.29.26)
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: Regulation and Potential Ban of Data Centers Dear Alderwoman Dimitrijevic:

This responds to your June 22, 2026 request for an opinion from the City Attorney’s Office regarding why the proposed substitute ordinance relating to the building of data centers (Common Council File No. 260142, proposed substitute A attached) is more advisable from a legal risk perspective than a ban on all data centers of any size in the city.
Data Centers Two particular attributes of data centers are essential to this analysis.
First, the term “data center” does not account for scale — a closet with half a dozen servers or a warehouse with ten thousand are both equally “data centers” at their core.

There are small data centers in a way that there are not small correctional facilities or material reclamation facilities, which are examples of uses in the city’s zoning code that are not permitted in any district.

Second, some would argue that data centers above a certain scale draw large quantities of power, generate significant amounts of noise, and require cooling systems that can waste vast amounts of water.

Because a “data center” includes uses so minor they could be freely done anywhere and so intense they might not be allowable anywhere in the city, regulation of data centers must reasonably account for both extremes, and its classifications must be supported by a record of reliable evidence.

Second, and more importantly, the proposed ordinance is more likely to withstand a legal challenge because it is tailored to address specific public welfare concerns that arise from the various types and sizes of data centers being regulated.

A court is more likely to find that the regulations in the proposed ordinance are designed to actually accomplish a purpose within the scope of the city’s police power, as opposed to a wholesale ban which fails to distinguish between data centers that pose little risk to the health, safety, or welfare of the public, and those that pose greater risk (whether because of their size, noise, or energy use).

Although only a few municipalities across the country have enacted complete bans on data centers, a lawsuit filed March 31, 2026 in Tennessee federal court by ExoticRidge Crypto Company against Hawkins County provides some insight into potential legal claims in response to a complete ban.
ExoticRidge alleges that Hawkins County violated the constitution by banning all data centers and cryptocurrency mining em masse, without regard to the actual impact of any particular project.

The text of the Hawkins County ban claims the massive amounts of electricity required to power cryptocurrency mining and large-scale data centers and the continuous industrial noise from the generators, cooling systems, and ventilation equipment are incompatible with the county’s rural character and the peaceful enjoyment of property by the county’s residents and that such operations typically create little to no sustainable economic benefit to the local community, employing minimal staff while imposing significant environmental and infrastructure burdens.

records.title: CPC Staff Report
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: This substitute ordinance would create a temporary pause in the establishment of new data centers or enlargement of existing data centers for one year, or until the Zoning Code is amended to formally define and regulate data centers.

This ordinance finds that the unprecedented recent national growth in the construction of data centers poses new and unique implications to communities, including impacts to energy and water infrastructure, the environment, and the public health, safety, and welfare.

Cities and states across the country are struggling to determine how to regulate this new and unique land use, and the Common Council intends for data centers to exist in harmony with the City’s existing Citywide Policy Plan, including the Climate & Equity Plan.

A separate Common Council File that would create a more long-term regulatory structure for data centers within the Zoning Code has been introduced and begun the process of public review and discussion (File No. 260142).
That separate ordinance would amend the City’s Zoning Code to establish a regulatory framework for data centers.

However, until that framework can be established, the sponsors of this pending pause ordinance seek to temporarily prohibit the building of new data centers until such time as the City’s Zoning Code is amended to accommodate this new type of land use.
At the present time, the City of Milwaukee’s Zoning Code does not specifically regulate data center land uses.

The proposed pause legislation is intended to serve as stopgap measure, allowing for the City to best protect public health, safety, and welfare, while working to establish a regulatory framework for data centers and to ensure future data center developments’ harmony with the City of Milwaukee’s Citywide Policy Plan and Climate & Equity Plan.

In this ordinance, “data center” means a facility, other than a transmission tower, used primarily to operate, maintain, or provide access to computer and network facilities for the transmission of voice, data, text, internet, sound, or full- motion-picture video between network termination points, together with accessory uses and facilities such as offices, air handlers, power generators, generator fuel storage, water cooling and storage facilities, and utility infrastructure that supports sustained operation of the data center.

Data center 251924 – 809 North Broadway, Milwaukee, WI 53202-3617 ZCTC Data Center Moratorium ● Phone (414) 286-5800 ● www.milwaukee.gov/dcd 09/28/26 CPC Milwaukee Business Information: www.choosemilwaukee.com shall not mean a computer server room or data facility that serves another principal use on the same premises.

No city department, board, commission, agency, or officer shall accept for filing, review, processing, or approval any application, permit request, occupancy request, zoning request, site-plan submission, or similar request seeking to establish, construct, enlarge, expand, convert, or occupy a data center during the effective period of this ordinance.

This prohibition shall apply regardless of how the facility is defined in the application materials, provided that the proposed principal use meets the definition of a data center, as defined in Part 1.

records.title: City Attorney Opinion on CCFN 260142 (6.29.26)
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: Regulation and Potential Ban of Data Centers Dear Alderwoman Dimitrijevic:

This responds to your June 22, 2026 request for an opinion from the City Attorney’s Office regarding why the proposed substitute ordinance relating to the building of data centers (Common Council File No. 260142, proposed substitute A attached) is more advisable from a legal risk perspective than a ban on all data centers of any size in the city.
Data Centers Two particular attributes of data centers are essential to this analysis.
First, the term “data center” does not account for scale — a closet with half a dozen servers or a warehouse with ten thousand are both equally “data centers” at their core.

There are small data centers in a way that there are not small correctional facilities or material reclamation facilities, which are examples of uses in the city’s zoning code that are not permitted in any district.

Second, some would argue that data centers above a certain scale draw large quantities of power, generate significant amounts of noise, and require cooling systems that can waste vast amounts of water.

Because a “data center” includes uses so minor they could be freely done anywhere and so intense they might not be allowable anywhere in the city, regulation of data centers must reasonably account for both extremes, and its classifications must be supported by a record of reliable evidence.

Second, and more importantly, the proposed ordinance is more likely to withstand a legal challenge because it is tailored to address specific public welfare concerns that arise from the various types and sizes of data centers being regulated.

A court is more likely to find that the regulations in the proposed ordinance are designed to actually accomplish a purpose within the scope of the city’s police power, as opposed to a wholesale ban which fails to distinguish between data centers that pose little risk to the health, safety, or welfare of the public, and those that pose greater risk (whether because of their size, noise, or energy use).

Although only a few municipalities across the country have enacted complete bans on data centers, a lawsuit filed March 31, 2026 in Tennessee federal court by ExoticRidge Crypto Company against Hawkins County provides some insight into potential legal claims in response to a complete ban.
ExoticRidge alleges that Hawkins County violated the constitution by banning all data centers and cryptocurrency mining em masse, without regard to the actual impact of any particular project.

The text of the Hawkins County ban claims the massive amounts of electricity required to power cryptocurrency mining and large-scale data centers and the continuous industrial noise from the generators, cooling systems, and ventilation equipment are incompatible with the county’s rural character and the peaceful enjoyment of property by the county’s residents and that such operations typically create little to no sustainable economic benefit to the local community, employing minimal staff while imposing significant environmental and infrastructure burdens.

records.title: CPC Staff Report
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: This substitute ordinance would create a temporary pause in the establishment of new data centers or enlargement of existing data centers for one year, or until the Zoning Code is amended to formally define and regulate data centers.

This ordinance finds that the unprecedented recent national growth in the construction of data centers poses new and unique implications to communities, including impacts to energy and water infrastructure, the environment, and the public health, safety, and welfare.

Cities and states across the country are struggling to determine how to regulate this new and unique land use, and the Common Council intends for data centers to exist in harmony with the City’s existing Citywide Policy Plan, including the Climate & Equity Plan.

A separate Common Council File that would create a more long-term regulatory structure for data centers within the Zoning Code has been introduced and begun the process of public review and discussion (File No. 260142).
That separate ordinance would amend the City’s Zoning Code to establish a regulatory framework for data centers.

However, until that framework can be established, the sponsors of this pending pause ordinance seek to temporarily prohibit the building of new data centers until such time as the City’s Zoning Code is amended to accommodate this new type of land use.
At the present time, the City of Milwaukee’s Zoning Code does not specifically regulate data center land uses.

The proposed pause legislation is intended to serve as stopgap measure, allowing for the City to best protect public health, safety, and welfare, while working to establish a regulatory framework for data centers and to ensure future data center developments’ harmony with the City of Milwaukee’s Citywide Policy Plan and Climate & Equity Plan.

In this ordinance, “data center” means a facility, other than a transmission tower, used primarily to operate, maintain, or provide access to computer and network facilities for the transmission of voice, data, text, internet, sound, or full- motion-picture video between network termination points, together with accessory uses and facilities such as offices, air handlers, power generators, generator fuel storage, water cooling and storage facilities, and utility infrastructure that supports sustained operation of the data center.

Data center 251924 – 809 North Broadway, Milwaukee, WI 53202-3617 ZCTC Data Center Moratorium ● Phone (414) 286-5800 ● www.milwaukee.gov/dcd 09/28/26 CPC Milwaukee Business Information: www.choosemilwaukee.com shall not mean a computer server room or data facility that serves another principal use on the same premises.

No city department, board, commission, agency, or officer shall accept for filing, review, processing, or approval any application, permit request, occupancy request, zoning request, site-plan submission, or similar request seeking to establish, construct, enlarge, expand, convert, or occupy a data center during the effective period of this ordinance.

This prohibition shall apply regardless of how the facility is defined in the application materials, provided that the proposed principal use meets the definition of a data center, as defined in Part 1.

records.title: MMAC Oppose
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: We appreciate the Council’s interest in establishing a clear framework for evaluating data center development, and we share the goal of ensuring that any project in Milwaukee is a good neighbor.

The ordinance establishes a one-year prohibition on accepting applications related to the establishment or development of data centers or continues prohibition until the City's zoning code is amended to specifically regulate data centers.

MMAC strongly opposes this proposal because a pause of up to one year would effectively shut Milwaukee out of new data center investment while other communities continue to compete for these projects.
Data centers are the physical backbone of the modern economy.

Billions of dollars in data center investment are now under construction or planned in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington, Beaver Dam, and other communities, generating thousands of construction jobs and transformative growth in local tax bases.

Earlier this year, the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin approved a rate structure requiring the largest data center customers to pay the full cost of the new generation and fuel needed to serve them, expressly protecting existing residential and business ratepayers.

Milwaukee needs sustained growth in its property tax base to fund the services residents depend on, and data centers are among the highest-value, lowest-service-demand land uses available, significant taxable investment that adds little burden on schools, streets, or public safety.

records.title: City Attorney Opinion on CCFN 260142 (6.29.26)
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: Regulation and Potential Ban of Data Centers Dear Alderwoman Dimitrijevic:

This responds to your June 22, 2026 request for an opinion from the City Attorney’s Office regarding why the proposed substitute ordinance relating to the building of data centers (Common Council File No. 260142, proposed substitute A attached) is more advisable from a legal risk perspective than a ban on all data centers of any size in the city.
Data Centers Two particular attributes of data centers are essential to this analysis.
First, the term “data center” does not account for scale — a closet with half a dozen servers or a warehouse with ten thousand are both equally “data centers” at their core.

There are small data centers in a way that there are not small correctional facilities or material reclamation facilities, which are examples of uses in the city’s zoning code that are not permitted in any district.

Second, some would argue that data centers above a certain scale draw large quantities of power, generate significant amounts of noise, and require cooling systems that can waste vast amounts of water.

Because a “data center” includes uses so minor they could be freely done anywhere and so intense they might not be allowable anywhere in the city, regulation of data centers must reasonably account for both extremes, and its classifications must be supported by a record of reliable evidence.

Second, and more importantly, the proposed ordinance is more likely to withstand a legal challenge because it is tailored to address specific public welfare concerns that arise from the various types and sizes of data centers being regulated.

A court is more likely to find that the regulations in the proposed ordinance are designed to actually accomplish a purpose within the scope of the city’s police power, as opposed to a wholesale ban which fails to distinguish between data centers that pose little risk to the health, safety, or welfare of the public, and those that pose greater risk (whether because of their size, noise, or energy use).

Although only a few municipalities across the country have enacted complete bans on data centers, a lawsuit filed March 31, 2026 in Tennessee federal court by ExoticRidge Crypto Company against Hawkins County provides some insight into potential legal claims in response to a complete ban.
ExoticRidge alleges that Hawkins County violated the constitution by banning all data centers and cryptocurrency mining em masse, without regard to the actual impact of any particular project.

The text of the Hawkins County ban claims the massive amounts of electricity required to power cryptocurrency mining and large-scale data centers and the continuous industrial noise from the generators, cooling systems, and ventilation equipment are incompatible with the county’s rural character and the peaceful enjoyment of property by the county’s residents and that such operations typically create little to no sustainable economic benefit to the local community, employing minimal staff while imposing significant environmental and infrastructure burdens.

records.title: CPC Staff Report
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: This substitute ordinance would create a temporary pause in the establishment of new data centers or enlargement of existing data centers for one year, or until the Zoning Code is amended to formally define and regulate data centers.

This ordinance finds that the unprecedented recent national growth in the construction of data centers poses new and unique implications to communities, including impacts to energy and water infrastructure, the environment, and the public health, safety, and welfare.

Cities and states across the country are struggling to determine how to regulate this new and unique land use, and the Common Council intends for data centers to exist in harmony with the City’s existing Citywide Policy Plan, including the Climate & Equity Plan.

A separate Common Council File that would create a more long-term regulatory structure for data centers within the Zoning Code has been introduced and begun the process of public review and discussion (File No. 260142).
That separate ordinance would amend the City’s Zoning Code to establish a regulatory framework for data centers.

However, until that framework can be established, the sponsors of this pending pause ordinance seek to temporarily prohibit the building of new data centers until such time as the City’s Zoning Code is amended to accommodate this new type of land use.
At the present time, the City of Milwaukee’s Zoning Code does not specifically regulate data center land uses.

The proposed pause legislation is intended to serve as stopgap measure, allowing for the City to best protect public health, safety, and welfare, while working to establish a regulatory framework for data centers and to ensure future data center developments’ harmony with the City of Milwaukee’s Citywide Policy Plan and Climate & Equity Plan.

In this ordinance, “data center” means a facility, other than a transmission tower, used primarily to operate, maintain, or provide access to computer and network facilities for the transmission of voice, data, text, internet, sound, or full- motion-picture video between network termination points, together with accessory uses and facilities such as offices, air handlers, power generators, generator fuel storage, water cooling and storage facilities, and utility infrastructure that supports sustained operation of the data center.

Data center 251924 – 809 North Broadway, Milwaukee, WI 53202-3617 ZCTC Data Center Moratorium ● Phone (414) 286-5800 ● www.milwaukee.gov/dcd 09/28/26 CPC Milwaukee Business Information: www.choosemilwaukee.com shall not mean a computer server room or data facility that serves another principal use on the same premises.

No city department, board, commission, agency, or officer shall accept for filing, review, processing, or approval any application, permit request, occupancy request, zoning request, site-plan submission, or similar request seeking to establish, construct, enlarge, expand, convert, or occupy a data center during the effective period of this ordinance.

This prohibition shall apply regardless of how the facility is defined in the application materials, provided that the proposed principal use meets the definition of a data center, as defined in Part 1.

records.title: City Attorney Opinion on CCFN 260142 (6.29.26)
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: Regulation and Potential Ban of Data Centers Dear Alderwoman Dimitrijevic:

This responds to your June 22, 2026 request for an opinion from the City Attorney’s Office regarding why the proposed substitute ordinance relating to the building of data centers (Common Council File No. 260142, proposed substitute A attached) is more advisable from a legal risk perspective than a ban on all data centers of any size in the city.
Data Centers Two particular attributes of data centers are essential to this analysis.
First, the term “data center” does not account for scale — a closet with half a dozen servers or a warehouse with ten thousand are both equally “data centers” at their core.

There are small data centers in a way that there are not small correctional facilities or material reclamation facilities, which are examples of uses in the city’s zoning code that are not permitted in any district.

Second, some would argue that data centers above a certain scale draw large quantities of power, generate significant amounts of noise, and require cooling systems that can waste vast amounts of water.

Because a “data center” includes uses so minor they could be freely done anywhere and so intense they might not be allowable anywhere in the city, regulation of data centers must reasonably account for both extremes, and its classifications must be supported by a record of reliable evidence.

Second, and more importantly, the proposed ordinance is more likely to withstand a legal challenge because it is tailored to address specific public welfare concerns that arise from the various types and sizes of data centers being regulated.

A court is more likely to find that the regulations in the proposed ordinance are designed to actually accomplish a purpose within the scope of the city’s police power, as opposed to a wholesale ban which fails to distinguish between data centers that pose little risk to the health, safety, or welfare of the public, and those that pose greater risk (whether because of their size, noise, or energy use).

Although only a few municipalities across the country have enacted complete bans on data centers, a lawsuit filed March 31, 2026 in Tennessee federal court by ExoticRidge Crypto Company against Hawkins County provides some insight into potential legal claims in response to a complete ban.
ExoticRidge alleges that Hawkins County violated the constitution by banning all data centers and cryptocurrency mining em masse, without regard to the actual impact of any particular project.

The text of the Hawkins County ban claims the massive amounts of electricity required to power cryptocurrency mining and large-scale data centers and the continuous industrial noise from the generators, cooling systems, and ventilation equipment are incompatible with the county’s rural character and the peaceful enjoyment of property by the county’s residents and that such operations typically create little to no sustainable economic benefit to the local community, employing minimal staff while imposing significant environmental and infrastructure burdens.

records.title: CPC Staff Report
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: This substitute ordinance would create a temporary pause in the establishment of new data centers or enlargement of existing data centers for one year, or until the Zoning Code is amended to formally define and regulate data centers.

This ordinance finds that the unprecedented recent national growth in the construction of data centers poses new and unique implications to communities, including impacts to energy and water infrastructure, the environment, and the public health, safety, and welfare.

Cities and states across the country are struggling to determine how to regulate this new and unique land use, and the Common Council intends for data centers to exist in harmony with the City’s existing Citywide Policy Plan, including the Climate & Equity Plan.

A separate Common Council File that would create a more long-term regulatory structure for data centers within the Zoning Code has been introduced and begun the process of public review and discussion (File No. 260142).
That separate ordinance would amend the City’s Zoning Code to establish a regulatory framework for data centers.

However, until that framework can be established, the sponsors of this pending pause ordinance seek to temporarily prohibit the building of new data centers until such time as the City’s Zoning Code is amended to accommodate this new type of land use.
At the present time, the City of Milwaukee’s Zoning Code does not specifically regulate data center land uses.

The proposed pause legislation is intended to serve as stopgap measure, allowing for the City to best protect public health, safety, and welfare, while working to establish a regulatory framework for data centers and to ensure future data center developments’ harmony with the City of Milwaukee’s Citywide Policy Plan and Climate & Equity Plan.

In this ordinance, “data center” means a facility, other than a transmission tower, used primarily to operate, maintain, or provide access to computer and network facilities for the transmission of voice, data, text, internet, sound, or full- motion-picture video between network termination points, together with accessory uses and facilities such as offices, air handlers, power generators, generator fuel storage, water cooling and storage facilities, and utility infrastructure that supports sustained operation of the data center.

Data center 251924 – 809 North Broadway, Milwaukee, WI 53202-3617 ZCTC Data Center Moratorium ● Phone (414) 286-5800 ● www.milwaukee.gov/dcd 09/28/26 CPC Milwaukee Business Information: www.choosemilwaukee.com shall not mean a computer server room or data facility that serves another principal use on the same premises.

No city department, board, commission, agency, or officer shall accept for filing, review, processing, or approval any application, permit request, occupancy request, zoning request, site-plan submission, or similar request seeking to establish, construct, enlarge, expand, convert, or occupy a data center during the effective period of this ordinance.

This prohibition shall apply regardless of how the facility is defined in the application materials, provided that the proposed principal use meets the definition of a data center, as defined in Part 1.

MMAC strongly opposes this proposal because a pause of up to one year would effectively shut Milwaukee out of new data center investment while other communities continue to compete for these projects.
Data centers are the physical backbone of the modern economy.

Billions of dollars in data center investment are now under construction or planned in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington, Beaver Dam, and other communities, generating thousands of construction jobs and transformative growth in local tax bases.

Earlier this year, the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin approved a rate structure requiring the largest data center customers to pay the full cost of the new generation and fuel needed to serve them, expressly protecting existing residential and business ratepayers.

records.title: City Attorney Opinion on CCFN 260142 (6.29.26)
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: Regulation and Potential Ban of Data Centers Dear Alderwoman Dimitrijevic:

This responds to your June 22, 2026 request for an opinion from the City Attorney’s Office regarding why the proposed substitute ordinance relating to the building of data centers (Common Council File No. 260142, proposed substitute A attached) is more advisable from a legal risk perspective than a ban on all data centers of any size in the city.
Data Centers Two particular attributes of data centers are essential to this analysis.
First, the term “data center” does not account for scale — a closet with half a dozen servers or a warehouse with ten thousand are both equally “data centers” at their core.

There are small data centers in a way that there are not small correctional facilities or material reclamation facilities, which are examples of uses in the city’s zoning code that are not permitted in any district.

Second, some would argue that data centers above a certain scale draw large quantities of power, generate significant amounts of noise, and require cooling systems that can waste vast amounts of water.

Because a “data center” includes uses so minor they could be freely done anywhere and so intense they might not be allowable anywhere in the city, regulation of data centers must reasonably account for both extremes, and its classifications must be supported by a record of reliable evidence.

Second, and more importantly, the proposed ordinance is more likely to withstand a legal challenge because it is tailored to address specific public welfare concerns that arise from the various types and sizes of data centers being regulated.

A court is more likely to find that the regulations in the proposed ordinance are designed to actually accomplish a purpose within the scope of the city’s police power, as opposed to a wholesale ban which fails to distinguish between data centers that pose little risk to the health, safety, or welfare of the public, and those that pose greater risk (whether because of their size, noise, or energy use).

Although only a few municipalities across the country have enacted complete bans on data centers, a lawsuit filed March 31, 2026 in Tennessee federal court by ExoticRidge Crypto Company against Hawkins County provides some insight into potential legal claims in response to a complete ban.
ExoticRidge alleges that Hawkins County violated the constitution by banning all data centers and cryptocurrency mining em masse, without regard to the actual impact of any particular project.

The text of the Hawkins County ban claims the massive amounts of electricity required to power cryptocurrency mining and large-scale data centers and the continuous industrial noise from the generators, cooling systems, and ventilation equipment are incompatible with the county’s rural character and the peaceful enjoyment of property by the county’s residents and that such operations typically create little to no sustainable economic benefit to the local community, employing minimal staff while imposing significant environmental and infrastructure burdens.

records.title: CPC Staff Report
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: This substitute ordinance would create a temporary pause in the establishment of new data centers or enlargement of existing data centers for one year, or until the Zoning Code is amended to formally define and regulate data centers.

This ordinance finds that the unprecedented recent national growth in the construction of data centers poses new and unique implications to communities, including impacts to energy and water infrastructure, the environment, and the public health, safety, and welfare.

Cities and states across the country are struggling to determine how to regulate this new and unique land use, and the Common Council intends for data centers to exist in harmony with the City’s existing Citywide Policy Plan, including the Climate & Equity Plan.

A separate Common Council File that would create a more long-term regulatory structure for data centers within the Zoning Code has been introduced and begun the process of public review and discussion (File No. 260142).
That separate ordinance would amend the City’s Zoning Code to establish a regulatory framework for data centers.

However, until that framework can be established, the sponsors of this pending pause ordinance seek to temporarily prohibit the building of new data centers until such time as the City’s Zoning Code is amended to accommodate this new type of land use.
At the present time, the City of Milwaukee’s Zoning Code does not specifically regulate data center land uses.

The proposed pause legislation is intended to serve as stopgap measure, allowing for the City to best protect public health, safety, and welfare, while working to establish a regulatory framework for data centers and to ensure future data center developments’ harmony with the City of Milwaukee’s Citywide Policy Plan and Climate & Equity Plan.

In this ordinance, “data center” means a facility, other than a transmission tower, used primarily to operate, maintain, or provide access to computer and network facilities for the transmission of voice, data, text, internet, sound, or full- motion-picture video between network termination points, together with accessory uses and facilities such as offices, air handlers, power generators, generator fuel storage, water cooling and storage facilities, and utility infrastructure that supports sustained operation of the data center.

Data center 251924 – 809 North Broadway, Milwaukee, WI 53202-3617 ZCTC Data Center Moratorium ● Phone (414) 286-5800 ● www.milwaukee.gov/dcd 09/28/26 CPC Milwaukee Business Information: www.choosemilwaukee.com shall not mean a computer server room or data facility that serves another principal use on the same premises.

No city department, board, commission, agency, or officer shall accept for filing, review, processing, or approval any application, permit request, occupancy request, zoning request, site-plan submission, or similar request seeking to establish, construct, enlarge, expand, convert, or occupy a data center during the effective period of this ordinance.

This prohibition shall apply regardless of how the facility is defined in the application materials, provided that the proposed principal use meets the definition of a data center, as defined in Part 1.

records.title: MMAC Oppose
records.item: A substitute ordinance relating to a temporary pause in the establishment and development of data centers. 251924
sentences: We appreciate the Council’s interest in establishing a clear framework for evaluating data center development, and we share the goal of ensuring that any project in Milwaukee is a good neighbor.

The ordinance establishes a one-year prohibition on accepting applications related to the establishment or development of data centers or continues prohibition until the City's zoning code is amended to specifically regulate data centers.

MMAC strongly opposes this proposal because a pause of up to one year would effectively shut Milwaukee out of new data center investment while other communities continue to compete for these projects.
Data centers are the physical backbone of the modern economy.

Billions of dollars in data center investment are now under construction or planned in Mount Pleasant, Port Washington, Beaver Dam, and other communities, generating thousands of construction jobs and transformative growth in local tax bases.

Earlier this year, the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin approved a rate structure requiring the largest data center customers to pay the full cost of the new generation and fuel needed to serve them, expressly protecting existing residential and business ratepayers.

Milwaukee needs sustained growth in its property tax base to fund the services residents depend on, and data centers are among the highest-value, lowest-service-demand land uses available, significant taxable investment that adds little burden on schools, streets, or public safety.

The Plan Commission is considering adoption of the Alliant Energy Center master plan.

The applicant is seeking approvals to rezone two areas of the Alliant Energy Center to RMX for future development, though no development is proposed at this time.

All recommendations are subject to input at the public hearing. • That the Plan Commission forward the Alliant Energy Center master plan to Common Council with a recommendation to adopt the associated resolution; and • That if the Plan Commission forwards the master plan to Council for approval, that it find the standards for zoning map amendments are met and forward the zoning map amendments generally located at 34 Fairgrounds Drive from PR to RMX to Common Council with a recommendation to approve.

The greater Alliant Energy Center is approximately 164 acres and generally bounded by East Olin Avenue on the north, John Nolen Drive and Rimrock Road on the east, East Rusk Avenue on the south, and Rusk Avenue and Expo Way on the west.

The two areas of the Alliant Energy Center proposed to be rezoned are located at the far northern corner of the site at the corner of East Olin Avenue and Expo Way and at the far eastern corner of the site between West Expo Drive and Alliant Energy Way.

The Alliant Energy Center is zoned PR (Parks and Recreation district) and developed with five primary buildings, including the Coliseum, two New Holland Pavilions, and Exhibition Hall, and Arena building, as well as several smaller buildings.

The applicant has also submitted a master plan for the Alliant Energy Center for City review and adoption.
The purpose of the master plan is to guide the future development of the Alliant Energy Center campus by establishing a long-term land use and development framework.

sentences: Authorizing electric service agreements for the purchase of backup generation service with Madison Gas & Electric Company, including the installation of a standby generator, on Madison Water Utility facility sites RECOMMENDATION Staff recommend authorizing electric service agreements for the purchase of backup generation service with Madison Gas & Electric Company (MGE), including the installation of a standby generator, on Madison Water Utility (MWU) facility sites.
BACKGROUND MWU’s water supply runs primarily on its pumps, which run on electricity, and reliability is significantly improved with on-site standby generation where possible.
MWU and MGE have multiple ongoing arrangements in place that provide MGE standby generators at MWU facilities.
Future generators may also be offered to MWU by MGE for similar purposes, at mutually beneficial MWU facility locations to be determined.
These arrangements are subject to Wisconsin Public Service Commission (PSC) oversight through MGE’s Backup Generation Service (BGS) tariff.
The results are reduced costs for MWU compared to the costs that MWU would otherwise need to account for to outright own, operate, and maintain their own generator at any given facility.

records.title: 91135 Body
records.item: Creating Section 28.140 to establish a temporary moratorium on the consideration and/or issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers and amending 28.061, 28.082, and 28.151 to accommodate the temporary moratorium. Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data & Teleco
sentences: This proposed ordinance creates a temporary moratorium on issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers of more than 10,000 square feet of floor area.

Data centers are facilities, contained within a single building or in a collection of buildings, used primarily for the storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital data, which primarily houses computer or network equipment, systems, servers, appliances and other associated components related to digital data operations.
The facility may also include utility infrastructure to support sustained operations at the data center.
Currently, Madison’s zoning code (MGO Chapter 28) does not include a definition or specific standards for ‘data centers’ as a use category.

While our community and economy benefit from data storage, research studies and observations in other communities show that certain large-scale data centers may pose a significant strain on energy, water use, emergency services, traffic, noise, air quality and urban development challenges that require planning and consideration.

Without a zoning regulation that reflects current best practices to responsibly manage this use, the construction of new data centers may affect property values, the implementation of the City’s long-range land use plans, and be detrimental to the public health, safety and general welfare.
Therefore, a twelve (12) month moratorium is necessary to research and establish well-informed, consistent zoning and/or regulatory standards applied to data centers and telecommunications centers.

The moratorium will allow the City of Madison agencies, including the Office of the City Attorney (“OCA”) and the Department of Planning and Economic Development (“DPCED”), to research best practices and safeguards, including creating a definition of data centers, and other use types if needed; identify the specific planning and development considerations relevant to our community for the responsible operation of data centers in the future; and propose potential standards.

Additionally, a twelve (12) month moratorium will allow the City of Madison to gain insights from the newly created Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers for the purposes of regional coordination. *********************************************************************************** The Common Council of the City of Madison do hereby ordain as follows: 1.

Section 28.140 entitled “Temporary Moratorium on Data Centers and Telecommunications Centers” of the Madison General Ordinances is created as follows: “28.140 TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON DATA CENTERS AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS CENTERS.

A temporary moratorium is hereby declared with respect to the issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers, as a principal and primary use, when they have a floor area greater than 10,000 square feet contained within a single building or collection of buildings.

The purpose of the moratorium is to provide the City of Madison with adequate time to assess the impacts and secondary effects of data centers and telecommunications centers and promote meaningful development and implementation of Madison General Ordinances with regard to both.

records.title: Zoning Text Memo - Data Center Moratorium
records.item: Creating Section 28.140 to establish a temporary moratorium on the consideration and/or issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers and amending 28.061, 28.082, and 28.151 to accommodate the temporary moratorium. Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data & Teleco
sentences: Zoning Text Amendment Legistar File ID #: 91135 (Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data Centers & Telecommunications Centers) Prepared By:

Zoning and Planning Staff Background and Purpose This proposed ordinance creates a temporary moratorium, for up to 12 months, on the issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers with a floor area greater than 10,000 sq.ft. as a principal and primary use.

While our community and economy can benefit from data storage, research studies and experience from other communities show that certain large-scale data centers may pose a significant strain on energy and water use, emergency services, traffic, noise, air quality and urban development challenges that require planning and consideration.

Without a zoning regulation that reflects current best practices to responsibly manage this use, the construction of new data centers may impact the implementation of the City’s longrange land use plans, affect property values, or be detrimental to the public health, safety and general welfare.
A moratorium is necessary to research and establish well-informed, consistent zoning and/or other local regulatory standards to be applied to data centers and telecommunications centers.

The moratorium will allow the City of Madison agencies, including the Office of the City Attorney (“OCA”) and the Department of Planning and Economic Development (“DPCED”), to research best practices and safeguards, including creating a permanent definition of data centers and/or creating or updating other use types if needed; identifying the specific planning and development considerations relevant to our community for the responsible operation of data centers in the future; and proposing potential zoning or other local ordinance standards for the operation of these uses within the city.

It is anticipated that this will involve consultation with other municipalities, experts and stakeholders; include a review of relevant available studies and research pertaining to effective municipal regulation of data centers; and provide opportunities for public participation.
Additionally, a 12-month moratorium will allow the City of Madison to gain insights from the newly created Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers for regional coordination.

Scope of Moratorium Moratorium on New Data Centers or Telecommunications Centers This ordinance pertains to zoning certificates for new data centers or telecommunications centers of greater than 10,000 sq.ft. in floor area within the City of Madison.

The facility may also include air handlers, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, and other associated utility infrastructure to support sustained operations at the data center.

sentences: This proposed ordinance creates a temporary moratorium on issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers of more than 10,000 square feet of floor area.

Data centers are facilities, contained within a single building or in a collection of buildings, used primarily for the storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital data, which primarily houses computer or network equipment, systems, servers, appliances and other associated components related to digital data operations.
The facility may also include utility infrastructure to support sustained operations at the data center.
Currently, Madison’s zoning code (MGO Chapter 28) does not include a definition or specific standards for ‘data centers’ as a use category.

While our community and economy benefit from data storage, research studies and observations in other communities show that certain large-scale data centers may pose a significant strain on energy, water use, emergency services, traffic, noise, air quality and urban development challenges that require planning and consideration.

Without a zoning regulation that reflects current best practices to responsibly manage this use, the construction of new data centers may affect property values, the implementation of the City’s long-range land use plans, and be detrimental to the public health, safety and general welfare.
Therefore, a twelve (12) month moratorium is necessary to research and establish well-informed, consistent zoning and/or regulatory standards applied to data centers and telecommunications centers.

The moratorium will allow the City of Madison agencies, including the Office of the City Attorney (“OCA”) and the Department of Planning and Economic Development (“DPCED”), to research best practices and safeguards, including creating a definition of data centers, and other use types if needed; identify the specific planning and development considerations relevant to our community for the responsible operation of data centers in the future; and propose potential standards.

Additionally, a twelve (12) month moratorium will allow the City of Madison to gain insights from the newly created Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers for the purposes of regional coordination. *********************************************************************************** The Common Council of the City of Madison do hereby ordain as follows: 1.

Section 28.140 entitled “Temporary Moratorium on Data Centers and Telecommunications Centers” of the Madison General Ordinances is created as follows: “28.140 TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON DATA CENTERS AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS CENTERS.

A temporary moratorium is hereby declared with respect to the issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers, as a principal and primary use, when they have a floor area greater than 10,000 square feet contained within a single building or collection of buildings.

The purpose of the moratorium is to provide the City of Madison with adequate time to assess the impacts and secondary effects of data centers and telecommunications centers and promote meaningful development and implementation of Madison General Ordinances with regard to both.

records.item: Creating Section 28.140 to establish a temporary moratorium on the consideration and/or issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers and amending 28.061, 28.082, and 28.151 to accommodate the temporary moratorium. Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data & Teleco
sentences: Zoning Text Amendment Legistar File ID #: 91135 (Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data Centers & Telecommunications Centers) Prepared By:

Zoning and Planning Staff Background and Purpose This proposed ordinance creates a temporary moratorium, for up to 12 months, on the issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers with a floor area greater than 10,000 sq.ft. as a principal and primary use.

While our community and economy can benefit from data storage, research studies and experience from other communities show that certain large-scale data centers may pose a significant strain on energy and water use, emergency services, traffic, noise, air quality and urban development challenges that require planning and consideration.

Without a zoning regulation that reflects current best practices to responsibly manage this use, the construction of new data centers may impact the implementation of the City’s longrange land use plans, affect property values, or be detrimental to the public health, safety and general welfare.
A moratorium is necessary to research and establish well-informed, consistent zoning and/or other local regulatory standards to be applied to data centers and telecommunications centers.

The moratorium will allow the City of Madison agencies, including the Office of the City Attorney (“OCA”) and the Department of Planning and Economic Development (“DPCED”), to research best practices and safeguards, including creating a permanent definition of data centers and/or creating or updating other use types if needed; identifying the specific planning and development considerations relevant to our community for the responsible operation of data centers in the future; and proposing potential zoning or other local ordinance standards for the operation of these uses within the city.

It is anticipated that this will involve consultation with other municipalities, experts and stakeholders; include a review of relevant available studies and research pertaining to effective municipal regulation of data centers; and provide opportunities for public participation.
Additionally, a 12-month moratorium will allow the City of Madison to gain insights from the newly created Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers for regional coordination.

Scope of Moratorium Moratorium on New Data Centers or Telecommunications Centers This ordinance pertains to zoning certificates for new data centers or telecommunications centers of greater than 10,000 sq.ft. in floor area within the City of Madison.
Currently, Madison’s zoning code (Madison General Ordinance, Chapter 28) does not include a definition or specific standards for ‘data centers’ as a use category.

The facility may also include air handlers, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, and other associated utility infrastructure to support sustained operations at the data center.

Data centers may also contain accessory office uses necessary to monitor and manage sustained operations at the data center.” (MGO 28.140) For the purposes of this moratorium, telecommunications centers are defined as they currently are in the zoning code, as “an office facility that is responsible for transmission, receipt, acceptance, processing, and distribution of incoming and outgoing communications.” (28.140 and 28.211) This moratorium does not apply to data centers or telecommunications centers that serve another principal or primary use allowed on the zoning lot.

records.item: Data Center Moratorium Update 93441
sentences: Overview of Draft Data Center Regulation Framework Date:

September 25, 2026 Recommended Zoning Framework Overview At this time, staff recommends the following framework for zoning regulations related to data centers: • Create three data center uses based on size, as defined below.

The recommended framework would include a maximum data center size limit of 100,000 sq. ft. and allow only one data center on a property. • All data center types are a permitted use; however, supplemental regulations and limits on where certain data center types are allowed will help control for the predominant land use/development concerns for each data center type. • Additional regulation would limit allowance for data centers in the TOD Overlay District, where housing and transit-supportive mixed-use development is a policy priority.

Together with other recommended supplemental regulations outlined in this memo, these data center types would exclude data center developments commonly referred to as “hyperscale” or a “data center campus” primarily by limiting the size and number of data centers.

Data Center Types & Associated Land Use/Development Concerns Staff has proposed the following data center definition: • Data Center - A facility used for the storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital data, which houses computer or network equipment, systems, servers, appliances and other associated components related to digital data operations.
The recommended zoning framework would further define three data center types.

Staff have recommended zoning districts where they may be allowed and other supplemental regulations intended to mitigate the land use concerns that have been identified. • Small Data Center o A data center that is less than 10,000 square feet contained within a single building. o These types of data centers are often a tenant in a building and support a single user or multiple users.
This includes businesses that lease space on their servers for off-site customers, such as the data center at 4916 E Broadway.

At larger sizes, they are more likely to house infrastructure that could support AI functions. o Primary land use concerns: an abundance of these data centers displacing land/buildings that are more suitable to other forms of employment/commercial uses and noise impacts associated with mechanical equipment, particularly in locations in close proximity to current or planned residential uses.
Statewide, there have been a number of very large and “hyperscale” data centers proposed or developed in recent years.
As noted, such data center types would not be permitted by the proposed framework.

Zoning Districts The following chart summarizes the recommended framework for the zoning districts each data center type could be allowed in: • Small Data Centers would be allowed in mixed-use, downtown, commercial, campus- institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below. • Medium Data Centers would be allowed in suburban employment areas, campus-institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below.

sentences: Overview of Draft Data Center Regulation Framework Date:

September 25, 2026 (Correction to supplemental regulation table made on October 7, 2026) Recommended Zoning Framework Overview At this time, staff recommends the following framework for zoning regulations related to data centers: • Create three data center uses based on size, as defined below.

The recommended framework would include a maximum data center size limit of 100,000 sq. ft. and allow only one data center on a property. • All data center types are a permitted use; however, supplemental regulations and limits on where certain data center types are allowed will help control for the predominant land use/development concerns for each data center type. • Additional regulation would limit allowance for data centers in the TOD Overlay District, where housing and transit-supportive mixed-use development is a policy priority.

Together with other recommended supplemental regulations outlined in this memo, these data center types would exclude data center developments commonly referred to as “hyperscale” or a “data center campus” primarily by limiting the size and number of data centers.

Data Center Types & Associated Land Use/Development Concerns Staff has proposed the following data center definition: • Data Center - A facility used for the storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital data, which houses computer or network equipment, systems, servers, appliances and other associated components related to digital data operations.
The recommended zoning framework would further define three data center types.

Staff have recommended zoning districts where they may be allowed and other supplemental regulations intended to mitigate the land use concerns that have been identified. • Small Data Center o A data center that is less than 10,000 square feet contained within a single building. o These types of data centers are often a tenant in a building and support a single user or multiple users.
This includes businesses that lease space on their servers for off-site customers, such as the data center at 4916 E Broadway.

At larger sizes, they are more likely to house infrastructure that could support AI functions. o Primary land use concerns: an abundance of these data centers displacing land/buildings that are more suitable to other forms of employment/commercial uses and noise impacts associated with mechanical equipment, particularly in locations in close proximity to current or planned residential uses.
Statewide, there have been a number of very large and “hyperscale” data centers proposed or developed in recent years.
As noted, such data center types would not be permitted by the proposed framework.

Zoning Districts The following chart summarizes the recommended framework for the zoning districts each data center type could be allowed in: • Small Data Centers would be allowed in mixed-use, downtown, commercial, campus- institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below. • Medium Data Centers would be allowed in suburban employment areas, campus-institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below.

records.item: Data Center Moratorium Update 93441
sentences: Madison’s Moratorium on Data Centers Is About To Expire — We Need a Permanent Moratorium on Data Centers!

The Decision Cannot Wait Madison’s one-year moratorium on new data centers is about to expire— and with it, an important opportunity to pause, gather the facts and protect our community’s long-term interests.

Data Centers Require Extraordinary Resources Nationally, data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023—approximately 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption— according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.
A 2024 Public Service Commission agreement for Microsoft’s Mount Pleasant facility included a 1,000-megawatt minimum demand commitment.
A continuous 1,000-megawatt load over a year would consume enough electricity to power roughly 1.27 million Wisconsin homes, based on the comparison cited in the proposal.

Require Full Disclosure Before Approval Before approving any project, Madison and Dane County should require disclosure of peak and annual electricity demand, water withdrawals and consumption, cooling technology, wastewater impacts, backup generation and infrastructure needs.
That uncertainty justifies a permanent moratorium while an independent, evidence-based study determines whether and under what conditions data centers are appropriate for our community.

sentences: PLANNING DIVISION STAFF REPORT July 27, 2026 PREPARED FOR THE PLAN COMMISSION Project Address: 110 East Rusk Avenue and 1919 Alliant Energy Center Way (District 14 – Alder Lieberman) Application Type:
Dane County Dept of Public Works, Highway, & Transportation; 1919 Alliant Energy Center Way;
The proposal includes minor site changes in the immediate area around the Exhibition Hall, but does not include the balance of the Alliant Energy Center.

The Planning Division recommends that the Plan Commission find that the standards for conditional uses are met and approve the conditional uses for a stadium, auditorium, or arena, and height in excess of the district maximum at 110 East Rusk Avenue and 1919 Alliant Energy Center Way subject to input at the public hearing and the conditions recommended by the reviewing agencies beginning on page 6.

The greater Alliant Energy Center is approximately 164 acres and generally bounded by East Olin Avenue on the north, John Nolen Drive and Rimrock Road on the east, East Rusk Avenue on the south, and Rusk Avenue and Expo Way on the west. 110 East Rusk Avenue, the parcel on which the Exhibition Center is built, is located at the south-central portion of the larger site; the building is located immediately south of Fairgrounds Drive.
Legistar File ID 93275 110 E Rusk Ave & 1919 Alliant Energy Center Way July 27, 2026 Page 2 Existing Conditions and Land Use:
The Alliant Energy Center is zoned PR (Parks and Recreation district) and developed with five primary buildings, as well as several smaller buildings.
Legistar File ID 93275 110 E Rusk Ave & 1919 Alliant Energy Center Way July 27, 2026 Page 3 Public Utilities and Services:
Project Description The applicant, representing Dane County and the Alliant Energy Center, is seeking approvals to expand the existing Exhibition Hall at the Alliant Energy Center.
This request represents the first phase of a planned implementation of a master plan for the entire Alliant Energy Center campus.

The Generalized Future Land Use map includes a note stating that, “the Alliant Energy Center is shown as SI, but may include restaurant, entertainment, and hotel uses if a Master Plan for the area that includes those uses is adopted by the City.
Such a Plan may include land use changes to surrounding properties.” The Alliant Energy Center is not included in any adopted special area plans.

records.title: 9-29-26 PC Draft Data Center Framework Memo.pdf
records.item: Data Center Moratorium Update 93441
sentences: Overview of Draft Data Center Regulation Framework Date:

September 25, 2026 Recommended Zoning Framework Overview At this time, staff recommends the following framework for zoning regulations related to data centers: • Create three data center uses based on size, as defined below.

The recommended framework would include a maximum data center size limit of 100,000 sq. ft. and allow only one data center on a property. • All data center types are a permitted use; however, supplemental regulations and limits on where certain data center types are allowed will help control for the predominant land use/development concerns for each data center type. • Additional regulation would limit allowance for data centers in the TOD Overlay District, where housing and transit-supportive mixed-use development is a policy priority.

Together with other recommended supplemental regulations outlined in this memo, these data center types would exclude data center developments commonly referred to as “hyperscale” or a “data center campus” primarily by limiting the size and number of data centers.

Data Center Types & Associated Land Use/Development Concerns Staff has proposed the following data center definition: • Data Center - A facility used for the storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital data, which houses computer or network equipment, systems, servers, appliances and other associated components related to digital data operations.
The recommended zoning framework would further define three data center types.

Staff have recommended zoning districts where they may be allowed and other supplemental regulations intended to mitigate the land use concerns that have been identified. • Small Data Center o A data center that is less than 10,000 square feet contained within a single building. o These types of data centers are often a tenant in a building and support a single user or multiple users.
This includes businesses that lease space on their servers for off-site customers, such as the data center at 4916 E Broadway.

At larger sizes, they are more likely to house infrastructure that could support AI functions. o Primary land use concerns: an abundance of these data centers displacing land/buildings that are more suitable to other forms of employment/commercial uses and noise impacts associated with mechanical equipment, particularly in locations in close proximity to current or planned residential uses.
Statewide, there have been a number of very large and “hyperscale” data centers proposed or developed in recent years.
As noted, such data center types would not be permitted by the proposed framework.

Zoning Districts The following chart summarizes the recommended framework for the zoning districts each data center type could be allowed in: • Small Data Centers would be allowed in mixed-use, downtown, commercial, campus- institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below. • Medium Data Centers would be allowed in suburban employment areas, campus-institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below.

sentences: Madison’s Moratorium on Data Centers Is About To Expire — We Need a Permanent Moratorium on Data Centers!

The Decision Cannot Wait Madison’s one-year moratorium on new data centers is about to expire— and with it, an important opportunity to pause, gather the facts and protect our community’s long-term interests.

Data Centers Require Extraordinary Resources Nationally, data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023—approximately 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption— according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.
A 2024 Public Service Commission agreement for Microsoft’s Mount Pleasant facility included a 1,000-megawatt minimum demand commitment.
A continuous 1,000-megawatt load over a year would consume enough electricity to power roughly 1.27 million Wisconsin homes, based on the comparison cited in the proposal.

Require Full Disclosure Before Approval Before approving any project, Madison and Dane County should require disclosure of peak and annual electricity demand, water withdrawals and consumption, cooling technology, wastewater impacts, backup generation and infrastructure needs.
That uncertainty justifies a permanent moratorium while an independent, evidence-based study determines whether and under what conditions data centers are appropriate for our community.
