records.title: 9-29-26 PC Draft Data Center Framework Memo.pdf
records.item: Data Center Moratorium Update 93441
sentences: Overview of Draft Data Center Regulation Framework Date:

September 25, 2026 Recommended Zoning Framework Overview At this time, staff recommends the following framework for zoning regulations related to data centers: • Create three data center uses based on size, as defined below.

The recommended framework would include a maximum data center size limit of 100,000 sq. ft. and allow only one data center on a property. • All data center types are a permitted use; however, supplemental regulations and limits on where certain data center types are allowed will help control for the predominant land use/development concerns for each data center type. • Additional regulation would limit allowance for data centers in the TOD Overlay District, where housing and transit-supportive mixed-use development is a policy priority.

Together with other recommended supplemental regulations outlined in this memo, these data center types would exclude data center developments commonly referred to as “hyperscale” or a “data center campus” primarily by limiting the size and number of data centers.

Data Center Types & Associated Land Use/Development Concerns Staff has proposed the following data center definition: • Data Center - A facility used for the storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital data, which houses computer or network equipment, systems, servers, appliances and other associated components related to digital data operations.
The recommended zoning framework would further define three data center types.

Staff have recommended zoning districts where they may be allowed and other supplemental regulations intended to mitigate the land use concerns that have been identified. • Small Data Center o A data center that is less than 10,000 square feet contained within a single building. o These types of data centers are often a tenant in a building and support a single user or multiple users.
This includes businesses that lease space on their servers for off-site customers, such as the data center at 4916 E Broadway.

At larger sizes, they are more likely to house infrastructure that could support AI functions. o Primary land use concerns: an abundance of these data centers displacing land/buildings that are more suitable to other forms of employment/commercial uses and noise impacts associated with mechanical equipment, particularly in locations in close proximity to current or planned residential uses.
Statewide, there have been a number of very large and “hyperscale” data centers proposed or developed in recent years.
As noted, such data center types would not be permitted by the proposed framework.

Zoning Districts The following chart summarizes the recommended framework for the zoning districts each data center type could be allowed in: • Small Data Centers would be allowed in mixed-use, downtown, commercial, campus- institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below. • Medium Data Centers would be allowed in suburban employment areas, campus-institutional, and industrial areas, with limits noted below.

sentences: Madison’s Moratorium on Data Centers Is About To Expire — We Need a Permanent Moratorium on Data Centers!

The Decision Cannot Wait Madison’s one-year moratorium on new data centers is about to expire— and with it, an important opportunity to pause, gather the facts and protect our community’s long-term interests.

Data Centers Require Extraordinary Resources Nationally, data centers used about 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023—approximately 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption— according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.
A 2024 Public Service Commission agreement for Microsoft’s Mount Pleasant facility included a 1,000-megawatt minimum demand commitment.
A continuous 1,000-megawatt load over a year would consume enough electricity to power roughly 1.27 million Wisconsin homes, based on the comparison cited in the proposal.

Require Full Disclosure Before Approval Before approving any project, Madison and Dane County should require disclosure of peak and annual electricity demand, water withdrawals and consumption, cooling technology, wastewater impacts, backup generation and infrastructure needs.
That uncertainty justifies a permanent moratorium while an independent, evidence-based study determines whether and under what conditions data centers are appropriate for our community.

records.title: 91135 Body
records.item: Creating Section 28.140 to establish a temporary moratorium on the consideration and/or issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers and amending 28.061, 28.082, and 28.151 to accommodate the temporary moratorium. Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data & Teleco
sentences: This proposed ordinance creates a temporary moratorium on issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers of more than 10,000 square feet of floor area.

Data centers are facilities, contained within a single building or in a collection of buildings, used primarily for the storage, management, processing, and transmission of digital data, which primarily houses computer or network equipment, systems, servers, appliances and other associated components related to digital data operations.
The facility may also include utility infrastructure to support sustained operations at the data center.
Currently, Madison’s zoning code (MGO Chapter 28) does not include a definition or specific standards for ‘data centers’ as a use category.

While our community and economy benefit from data storage, research studies and observations in other communities show that certain large-scale data centers may pose a significant strain on energy, water use, emergency services, traffic, noise, air quality and urban development challenges that require planning and consideration.

Without a zoning regulation that reflects current best practices to responsibly manage this use, the construction of new data centers may affect property values, the implementation of the City’s long-range land use plans, and be detrimental to the public health, safety and general welfare.
Therefore, a twelve (12) month moratorium is necessary to research and establish well-informed, consistent zoning and/or regulatory standards applied to data centers and telecommunications centers.

The moratorium will allow the City of Madison agencies, including the Office of the City Attorney (“OCA”) and the Department of Planning and Economic Development (“DPCED”), to research best practices and safeguards, including creating a definition of data centers, and other use types if needed; identify the specific planning and development considerations relevant to our community for the responsible operation of data centers in the future; and propose potential standards.

Additionally, a twelve (12) month moratorium will allow the City of Madison to gain insights from the newly created Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers for the purposes of regional coordination. *********************************************************************************** The Common Council of the City of Madison do hereby ordain as follows: 1.

Section 28.140 entitled “Temporary Moratorium on Data Centers and Telecommunications Centers” of the Madison General Ordinances is created as follows: “28.140 TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON DATA CENTERS AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS CENTERS.

A temporary moratorium is hereby declared with respect to the issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers, as a principal and primary use, when they have a floor area greater than 10,000 square feet contained within a single building or collection of buildings.

The purpose of the moratorium is to provide the City of Madison with adequate time to assess the impacts and secondary effects of data centers and telecommunications centers and promote meaningful development and implementation of Madison General Ordinances with regard to both.

records.title: Zoning Text Memo - Data Center Moratorium
records.item: Creating Section 28.140 to establish a temporary moratorium on the consideration and/or issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers and amending 28.061, 28.082, and 28.151 to accommodate the temporary moratorium. Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data & Teleco
sentences: Zoning Text Amendment Legistar File ID #: 91135 (Moratorium on Zoning Certificates for Data Centers & Telecommunications Centers) Prepared By:

Zoning and Planning Staff Background and Purpose This proposed ordinance creates a temporary moratorium, for up to 12 months, on the issuance of zoning certificates for data centers and telecommunications centers with a floor area greater than 10,000 sq.ft. as a principal and primary use.

While our community and economy can benefit from data storage, research studies and experience from other communities show that certain large-scale data centers may pose a significant strain on energy and water use, emergency services, traffic, noise, air quality and urban development challenges that require planning and consideration.

Without a zoning regulation that reflects current best practices to responsibly manage this use, the construction of new data centers may impact the implementation of the City’s longrange land use plans, affect property values, or be detrimental to the public health, safety and general welfare.
A moratorium is necessary to research and establish well-informed, consistent zoning and/or other local regulatory standards to be applied to data centers and telecommunications centers.

The moratorium will allow the City of Madison agencies, including the Office of the City Attorney (“OCA”) and the Department of Planning and Economic Development (“DPCED”), to research best practices and safeguards, including creating a permanent definition of data centers and/or creating or updating other use types if needed; identifying the specific planning and development considerations relevant to our community for the responsible operation of data centers in the future; and proposing potential zoning or other local ordinance standards for the operation of these uses within the city.

It is anticipated that this will involve consultation with other municipalities, experts and stakeholders; include a review of relevant available studies and research pertaining to effective municipal regulation of data centers; and provide opportunities for public participation.
Additionally, a 12-month moratorium will allow the City of Madison to gain insights from the newly created Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers for regional coordination.

Scope of Moratorium Moratorium on New Data Centers or Telecommunications Centers This ordinance pertains to zoning certificates for new data centers or telecommunications centers of greater than 10,000 sq.ft. in floor area within the City of Madison.
Currently, Madison’s zoning code (Madison General Ordinance, Chapter 28) does not include a definition or specific standards for ‘data centers’ as a use category.

The facility may also include air handlers, power generators, water cooling and storage facilities, utility substations, and other associated utility infrastructure to support sustained operations at the data center.

Data centers may also contain accessory office uses necessary to monitor and manage sustained operations at the data center.” (MGO 28.140) For the purposes of this moratorium, telecommunications centers are defined as they currently are in the zoning code, as “an office facility that is responsible for transmission, receipt, acceptance, processing, and distribution of incoming and outgoing communications.” (28.140 and 28.211) This moratorium does not apply to data centers or telecommunications centers that serve another principal or primary use allowed on the zoning lot.

sentences: Dear members of the Madison Plan Commission, I write in strong support of Legistar 91135, which proposes a one-year moratorium on data centers and telecommunications centers with a floor area greater than 10,000 sq.ft. as a principal and primary use.

Some of these companies view Wisconsin as the "wild west," where they can promise municipalities financial benefits while there is essentially no legislative guidance about the impacts these massive data centers might have on our cities.

Please see the related information, please see this 5-page Clean Economy Coalition of Wisconsin Data Center framework document (released 12/18/2025 by the 40-member Clean Economy Coalition of Wisconsin) addressing the challenges facing all Wisconsin cities because huge wealthy artificial intelligence (AI) companies are now operating in an largely unregulated environment, competing for control of land and massive amounts of water and energy.

Because at this time there are no regulatory protections that, for example, prevent utilities from abandoning their stated renewable energy sources goals in order to meet the energy and water demands of these huge new customers, this document advocates for a state-wide pause on all decisions pertaining to new data center proposals until state leaders establish a strategic planning framework that integrates data center demands with Wisconsin’s clean energy and climate commitments, while also prioritizing energy affordability and safeguarding public health.

I am strongly in support of a minimum one-year moratorium on data centers of the size defined in the proposal.
YES on data center moratorium Date:
Dear Madison Planning Commission, I was delighted to see that you are considering putting a moratorium on the construction of data centers.

(I work at UW-Madison and encounter AI all the time now--its deficiencies are obvious.) The environmental and human mental/physical health aspects are also significant, both around the existence of new huge data centers and around unthinking insertion of AI into everything for little reason other than to justify inflated tech company share prices.
Please reject the imposition of unneeded and unwanted data centers that benefit nobody but a tiny number of already-wealthy people who don't even live here.

sentences: 1 2025 RES-205 2 ESTABLISHING THE DANE COUNTY ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON DATA CENTERS 3 4 Across the Midwest, technology companies and investment firms are making 5 unprecedented investments in large “hyperscale” data centers, designed to support the 6 rapid growth of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital commerce.

These 7 facilities—often housed in massive buildings hundreds of thousands of square feet in 8 size and clustered on “campuses” spanning hundreds of acres—require extraordinary 9 levels of electrical power and cooling infrastructure, among other resources. 10 11 Several large data center projects have already been announced or are under 12 consideration within Wisconsin, including in Port Washington, Mount Pleasant, 13 Menomonie, and the Town of Vienna in Dane County.

These important and 17 potentially irreversible development decisions need to be based on sound, factual 18 information, and communities need to be equipped with an understanding of what 19 decisions are within their power when responding to proposals for data center 20 developments. 21 22 These developments promise potential benefits but at the same time, they raise complex 23 questions about sustainability, resource use, impacts on ratepayers, and community 24 compatibility, among other issues.
Hyperscale data centers are among the most energy- 25 intensive types of land use, drawing hundreds of megawatts of power and potentially 26 requiring large volumes of water for cooling.

The county has been a state leader in 35 farmland preservation, resource protection, and comprehensive planning, adopting 36 policies that emphasize compact growth, intergovernmental cooperation, and the 37 stewardship of land and water resources. 38 39 Given these Dane County values and longstanding commitments, the question of 40 whether—and under what circumstances—hyperscale data centers should be located 41 within Dane County warrants careful study.
Noise, lighting, and other aesthetic and community character impacts associated 65 with large-scale data centers; 66 5.

Intergovernmental relations, including the potential for both competition and 77 cooperation among communities, as well as approaches for consistent evaluation 78 and siting of data centers among the county’s towns, cities, and villages; 79 10.

records.title: 2025 RES-205
records.item: ESTABLISHING THE DANE COUNTY ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON DATA CENTERS 2025 RES-205
sentences: 1 2025 RES-205 2 ESTABLISHING THE DANE COUNTY ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON DATA CENTERS 3 4 Across the Midwest, technology companies and investment firms are making 5 unprecedented investments in large “hyperscale” data centers, designed to support the 6 rapid growth of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital commerce.

These 7 facilities—often housed in massive buildings hundreds of thousands of square feet in 8 size and clustered on “campuses” spanning hundreds of acres—require extraordinary 9 levels of electrical power and cooling infrastructure, among other resources. 10 11 Several large data center projects have already been announced or are under 12 consideration within Wisconsin, including in Port Washington, Mount Pleasant, 13 Menomonie, and the Town of Vienna in Dane County.

These important and 17 potentially irreversible development decisions need to be based on sound, factual 18 information, and communities need to be equipped with an understanding of what 19 decisions are within their power when responding to proposals for data center 20 developments. 21 22 These developments promise potential benefits but at the same time, they raise complex 23 questions about sustainability, resource use, impacts on ratepayers, and community 24 compatibility, among other issues.
Hyperscale data centers are among the most energy- 25 intensive types of land use, drawing hundreds of megawatts of power and potentially 26 requiring large volumes of water for cooling.

The county has been a state leader in 35 farmland preservation, resource protection, and comprehensive planning, adopting 36 policies that emphasize compact growth, intergovernmental cooperation, and the 37 stewardship of land and water resources. 38 39 Given these Dane County values and longstanding commitments, the question of 40 whether—and under what circumstances—hyperscale data centers should be located 41 within Dane County warrants careful study.
Noise, lighting, and other aesthetic and community character impacts associated 65 with large-scale data centers; 66 5.

Intergovernmental relations, including the potential for both competition and 77 cooperation among communities, as well as approaches for consistent evaluation 78 and siting of data centers among the county’s towns, cities, and villages; 79 10.

Alliant Energy Center Provider:

WHEREAS COUNTY, whose address is 1919 Alliant Energy Center Way, Madison, WI 53713, desires to purchase services from PROVIDER for the purpose of providing on call electrical services for the Alliant Energy Center; and WHEREAS PROVIDER, whose address is W133N5030 Campbell Drive, Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin 53051, is able and willing to provide such services;
Pursuant to paragraph #1 of the Attached contract, the Provider shall provide electrician service to the Alliant Energy Center, located at 1919 Alliant Energy Center Way, Madison, WI 53713.

The Electrician labor may involve any of the buildings – Veteran’s Memorial Coliseum, Exhibition Hall, Conference Center, New Holland Pavilions, Arena, as well as all parking lots and open spaces on the Alliant Energy Center Campus. 2.
Provider shall maintain a fully stocked electrical service van that will accompany any of the electricians who perform work at the Alliant Energy Center.
Additional assistance may be required for the Midwest Horse Fair in April and the Dane County Fair in July as well as for other events or in the absence of the Alliant Energy Center electrician. 5.
Provider will not charge for training time to train its electricians in the Alliant Energy Center facility, systems and procedures. 6.
Provider's employees shall not use improper language or act in a loud, boisterous manner, or act in any inappropriate or improper manner as determined by the Alliant Energy Center. 13.

sentences: This legislation requires the Alliant Energy Center to explore the possibility of County Employees who do not work at the Alliant Energy Center to assist with Surge Cleaning at the Alliant Energy Center.

The Alliant Energy Center shall process and schedule employees who voluntarily sign-up for Surge Cleaning. 5.
Limited Term Employees are not able to sign-up for Surge Cleaning at the Alliant Energy Center.
Comp time is not available as compensation for Surge Cleaning at the Alliant Energy Center. 8.
The Alliant Energy Center will provide for all training for staff who sign up for Surge Cleaning. 9.

records.title: 2025 PRES-214
records.item: AN OVERVIEW OF HYPERSCALE DATA CENTERS IN WISCONSIN 2025 PRES-214
sentences: Hyperscale Data Centers in Wisconsin BY:

JOHN G HANSEN Scope and Objective of This Report • The report is intended to provide preliminary information to the newly- created Dane County Advisory Committee on Data Centers. • This subject is treated with nuance as this is a very new development that is still not fully researched or understood. • There is a significant amount of misinformation regarding data centers on the internet.
The public of Dane County deserves to be presented with well-researched, realistic facts concerning what a new data center could mean for their community.

What is a Hyperscale Data Center? • Data centers house large-scale computers known as GPUs that process and store data from all over the world. • As demand for artificial intelligence (AI) increases, tech companies are embracing economies of scale and building massive, “hyperscale” data centers. • While the U.S. government does not have a formal definition for a “hyperscale” data center, the International Data Corporation defines them as containing over 5,000 servers and utilizing over 10,000 feet of floor space. • For reference, 10,000 square feet is about two NBA basketball courts combined.
States with Tax Incentives for Data Centers Vs.

Other Environmental and Nuisance Concerns • While hyperscale data centers give off few carbon emissions on the campus itself, generating the significant amount of electricity it requires using fossil fuel energy can release significant emissions. • Most data centers have on-campus, diesel- powered backup generators to use in case electricity supply stops. • These are often tested monthly, releasing emissions while being extremely noisy. • Some data centers emit constant low-frequency noise that can have adverse health effects on nearby residents.

Case Study – Microsoft Data Center in Mount Pleasant Continued • Microsoft has invested significantly into this community through Community Benefit Agreements. • They have partnered with local environmental groups to restore prairie and wetland habitats in the area. • In partnership with the local Gateway Technical College, Microsoft has launched a “Datacenter Academy’ that will train over a thousand students for “High-demand data center roles”. • Microsoft has covered the cost of supplying electricity to their campus, taking potential burden off local taxpayers.

Next Steps • Since hyperscale data centers are a relatively new technology, long term data regarding their impact on the local environment and economy still needs to be collected and made publicly available. • While this report does provide a broad overview of subjects to focus on when considering the issue of hyperscale data centers, the additional resources and references contained within the bibliography may be helpful for further research. • This is an ongoing issue and it is important to monitor local news for developments regarding data centers in Wisconsin.

sentences: Dane County Minutes - Final Unless Amended by Committee Advisory Committee on Data Centers Consider:
Updates Pending Legislation Document At the first committee meeting, a request made to have a list of pending legislation related to data centers.

The county’s Legislative Lobbyist pulled together pending legislation regarding data centers, which is available on the Planning website: <https://www.danecountyplanning.com/ACDC> Staff will request for the Legislative Lobbyist to include a key to the document indicating what the colors on the document represent.

Guest Speakers There were 4 guests in attendance to provide perspective on the two main agenda topics: data center basics, and regulatory authorities and policy options available to local units of government.
Speakers were ACDC member and UW data center lead, Terry Bradshaw;

Data Center Basics Terry Bradshaw presented an overview of data centers, explaining that data centers are climate-controlled facilities that contain the servers and related equipment to store and process digital information and enable a wide range of digital and online services, including “cloud” and video streaming services, online banking, and Artificial Intelligence (AI).

He described key infrastructure elements (“anatomy” of a data center), including utility interconnection/substations, on-site electrical equipment (switchgear/transformers and batteries/Uninterrupted Power Supply), IT load (servers/storage), cooling systems (including open-loop cooling towers versus closed-loop dry coolers), fiber/network connectivity, and backup power systems (often diesel generators with on-site fuel storage).

Discussion ensued regarding types of hardware, climate control of data centers, history of data centers, maintenance of cooling systems, environmental impacts of maintenance, consideration of renewable energy to power data centers.

Dane County Page 2 Printed on 3/20/2026 Advisory Committee on Data Minutes - Final Unless Amended March 10, 2026 Centers by Committee 2025 DATA CENTER BASICS PRES-295 Attachments: 2025 PRES-295.pdf Dane County Page 3 Printed on 3/20/2026 Advisory Committee on Data Minutes - Final Unless Amended March 10, 2026 Centers by Committee 3.

Local Government and Policy Options Professor Brian Ohm presented on the Wisconsin policy and regulatory context affecting data centers and reviewed the range of local government tools available to address them.

Professor Ohm noted that data centers represent the latest in a long list of contentious land use issues like suburban shopping malls, wind/solar farms, and frac sand mining that local governments in Wisconsin have had to address and determine how to move forward.

State policy actions were highlighted, including 2023 Wisconsin Act 19 which created sales/use tax exemptions for “qualified data centers”, and 2025 Wisconsin Act 16 which provided an exemption to the 12% cap on Tax Increment Financing for data center host communities Port Washington and Beaver Dam.

sentences: I ask that you begin the process of restoring trust in county institutions by passing item 11.E and F to limit staff from utilizing NDAs for data center projects and establish a county committee to evaluate county impacts of data center developments.
No Data Center in Rock County.

A data center in Rock County threatens my parents' retirement -- which is stored in the value of their home and property, the beauty and integrity and sacredness of Rock County's wild lands, as well as the gathering place where my children interact with family, spend time off their phones in relationship to the land and people around them, and soak up traditions.
Not only do data centers threaten water, life, land, wildlife and protected wild places, and my parents' middle class ability to live with dignity as they age, they devalue rural ways of living.
These data centers are not happening in ways that honor life, and so they should be made to wait until they can do so -- or they should not happen at all.

Put a policy in place requiring regular public reports on the status of nondisclosure agreements that relate to projects proposing to use 50 mw of power Put in place an interim policy governing staff engagement regarding any new construction projects of 50 mw of power.

If reporter Dana Fulton had not broken the story in March of 2026 - NONE of us might have any idea that data centers developers were eyeing several different sites in Rock County until shovels went into the ground.

September 8th CBS Committee Agenda’s Data Center & NDA Resolutions DATE:

September 4, 2026 Since the Planning & Development Committee acted on the five proposed Data Center and Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) Resolutions during its July 23rd and August 13th meetings, I wanted to provide the following summary.

As you will read, the Planning & Development Committee’s actions ranged from unanimous to split votes. • Establishing the Rock County Advisory Committee for Data Centers This Resolution proposes establishing a 13-member Data Center Advisory Committee, which would be charged with studying the countywide impacts (i.e. namely the economic and environmental) generated by a hyperscale data center.
The report’s findings are intended to serve as a hyperscale data center planning and policy guidance resource.

The Planning & Development Committee unanimously approved this Resolution (5 Ayes, 0 Noes). • Limiting County Staff from Entering into Non-Disclosure Agreements Relating to Hyperscale Data Centers This Resolution creates a countywide ban, applicable to all County staff, with regards to entering into any type or form of a Non-Disclosure Agreement for any proposed Rock County hyperscale data center project.
It also defines what constitutes a hyperscale data center.

The Planning & Development Committee did not approve this Resolution (2 Ayes, 3 Noes). • Policy Requiring a Regular Public Report on the Status of Non-Disclosure Agreements This Resolution creates a public reporting requirement for County staff that have entered any existing and/or new hyperscale data center Non-Disclosure Agreements.

Page 31 of 60 • Interim Policy Governing Staff Engagement with Hyperscale Data Center Development Proposals This Resolution directs the County Administrator to create a policy that would ban or prohibit any County employee from working on any hyperscale data center project – for at least an 18-month period.

records.title: County Board Staff Committee 2026-09-08 Public Comment CBS
sentences: Dear County Board Staff Committee Members, Please accept the following as my public comment regarding the data center-related resolutions on this evening’s agenda.
I understand the concerns surrounding data centers, and I support appropriate safeguards and transparency.

Chair Bostwick and members of the Rock County Board Staff Committee, I write in support of Items 6H and 6J on your agenda, the resolutions limiting county staff from entering into NDAs with hyperscale data center developers and limiting county staff from encouraging hyperscale data center development.
As the State Senator representing most of Rock County, I have seen public opinion shift dramatically over the last year and a half on the issue of hyperscale data centers.

I am confident from public polling, my own legislative survey, and conversations in the community that the vast majority of our shared constituents either oppose hyperscale data centers outright or have strong concerns about them and want to pump the breaks on them to put in place strong regulations, repeal tax incentives, and ensure transparency and community benefit.

However, data center NDAs have come to be viewed as uniquely toxic, with significant public backlash, legislative efforts to limit them, and some data center developers proactively ending the use of NDAs.

I first became aware of the proposed data center in the Town of Beloit when a reporter uncovered it, and I was shocked to find out that the project had been around for over a year, shielded by an NDA while everyone was publicly debating a different proposed data center in Janesville.
When I found out about this issue, I added my name to bipartisan legislation to ban staff and elected officials from signing NDAs to hide data center projects statewide.

I encourage Rock County to adopt a similar policy as outlined in Item 6H to build trust with residents and ensure that any future data center proposals in our community are considered with full transparency from the outset.

To be clear, this does not mean that every detail of a project must be revealed or that trade secrets cannot be shielded, but the public has a right to know if a hyperscale data center is being considered, who the developer is, and what role their local governments are playing.
I also believe it is wise for Rock County to stop soliciting or encouraging or playing quarterback for hyperscale data center projects, as Item 6J would direct.

All of the communities in Rock County where we know of potential data center development have pulled back from those projects, with many of these municipalities, and others, passing 12 or 18 month moratoriums as allowed under state law.

I demand that Rock County abstain from signing any non disclosure agreements (NDAs) with companies of massive size such as data centers and keep the public informed timely.
We wish to join the many residents demanding transparency from the County Board with respect to the now 4 proposed data centers and request NO NDAs be signed with them.
Until you do this -publicly- and balance both sides, you cannot convince the public that data centers are in our best interests.
As a resident of Center township, I am writing to state my strong opposition to the proposed data center at Fenrick and Polzin.
Data centers primarily use fossil fuels, which will degrade our local air and water quality.
Noise generated by data centers can extend up to a 2.5 mile radius, disrupting the lives of residents and harming wildlife.
I am requesting a ban on non-disclosure agreements regarding any potential or actual development of data centers or similar projects that would have a massive impact on the region.
Data center developers should not be allowed back door deals and secretive discussions, especially when the potential impact would be so hugely harmful to the region and beyond.
I do not want the few to get rich on the backs of us who would suffer from any type of data center project.
The majority do not want secretive dealings or data centers.

One-Year Data Center Moratorium Resolution Purpose The attached resolution establishes a temporary one-year moratorium on new data center development applications while the City evaluates potential impacts and develops appropriate policies.

What the Resolution Does • Creates a temporary pause on new data center approvals. • Allows staff, commissions, and the Council time to study best practices. • Provides an opportunity for public input and stakeholder engagement. • Enables the City to evaluate infrastructure, utility, zoning, financial impact, health, and land-use considerations before proposals are submitted.
What the Resolution Does Not Do • It is not a permanent ban on data centers. • It does not reject any specific project.
(I am unaware of any current proposal) • It does not prohibit future data center development. • It does not establish new regulations or zoning standards.
Data centers are a rapidly growing land use that can have significant impacts on electricity demand, utility infrastructure, water use, site selection, and long-term planning.
Taking time to evaluate data center development now may help avoid future conflicts and provide greater certainty for both residents and potential developers.

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Common Council of the City of Superior that a temporary moratorium is hereby established on the acceptance, processing, approval, and issuance of permits, licenses, zoning approvals, conditional use permits, site plans, or other development approvals for new data center developments within the City of Superior.

sentences: The Common Council is being asked to review and approve a proposed text amendment to the City of Port Washington Zoning Code that will add a new industrial district to its zoning code for the purpose of accommodating and regulating possible data center development.
A large area of land in the Town of Port Washington is currently under consideration for possible acquisition and development of a data center complex.
Should the project move forward, Cloverleaf Infrastructure is proposing to annex and acquire those lands into the city of Port Washington prior to any development for data center uses.

Considering such a development proposal, the City of Port Washington has determined its current zoning code, specifically its industrial district provisions, are not adequate to address the site demands of a large- scale data center campus because the City and its zoning consultants at the time did not envision such uses when much of the code was created decades ago.

Whether or not a data center complex in the city of Port Washington becomes a reality, planning staff has been involved with drafting zoning standards on the front end to ensure proper site development standards are in place should a data center proposal (or any future tech-centered projects) move forward.

Borchardt mentioned that the Village received a partial site plan application from Concordia Wireless on behalf of T-Mobile for the installation of a backup generator for their cellular antenna station located next to the water tower at Tower Park, 527 1st Street.

Motioned by Mortensen/Schremp to Approve the Partial Site Plan Application for the Installation of a Backup Generator at the Water Tower Located at 527 1st Street as Recommended with Concordia Wireless/T-Mobile Install New 8’ Fence Panels on AT&T’s Portion and Update the Landscaping Pending the Approval of the Agreement.
Therefore, the new rent, after the installation of the additional backup generator (240 sq. ft.) would be a monthly revenue of $2,241.41, with a 4% annual growth factor.
